item.title: Accountability isn't an event
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Leaders and their managers agree on what leaders are worst at. Knowing hasn't fixed it
item.category: Winning feels like a near miss
item.content:encoded:
Leaders and the managers who report to them disagree about almost everything Gallup measured. They agree on one thing: what leaders are worst at.

In a new Gallup study, Jim Harter and Corey Tatel asked both groups to rate leaders on seven competencies: building relationships, developing people, leading change, inspiring others, thinking critically, communicating clearly, and creating accountability. Creating accountability came last. For both groups.

46% of leaders rate themselves exceptional or outstanding at it.

30% of managers say the same about their own leader.

That 16-point gap sounds large until you see the rest. On six of the seven competencies, managers rate their leaders at least 20 points below the leaders’ own ratings. Accountability is where the two groups come closest.

So leaders still overrate themselves here, just by less than anywhere else. They can see the weakness. Their managers see it too. And seeing it hasn’t fixed it.

The problem isn’t awareness

That matters for how organizations try to fix it. Most develop managers through events: a two-day course, an assessment, a box checked before the budget year closes. A course can teach a skill. It can’t make one stick. And you can’t train your way out of a weakness everyone in the room can already see.

What I hear when leaders describe accountability

I coach about 20 executives and work with about 10 organizations. When I ask a senior leader how they hold their managers accountable, the answer almost always arrives as a story about a moment. A missed quarter. A hard conversation. A performance plan.

Almost nobody describes a Tuesday.

That’s the tell. Accountability, as most leaders practice it, happens after something has already gone wrong. So the manager on the other side only meets it when something is broken. In schools, it even has a season. Department chairs and division heads meet accountability at evaluation time, and the rest of the year it lives in good intentions.

The band doesn’t get tight at the clinic

Any working musician knows the difference between a clinic and a rehearsal. I used to play in a faculty band and work with student bands after school. A clinic teaches you something. Rehearsal is where the band actually locks in, every week, in a room where nobody is paying. The part I always loved was the listening. Everyone in the ensemble listens to everyone else, for cues, for tuning, for knowing you’re in the refrain and not the bridge. That’s where the dragged tempo and the missed change get fixed, while they’re small and cheap.

Last month, U2 marked fifty years together by going back to the Dublin school where it started. In September 1976, a 14-year-old drummer pinned a note to the school noticeboard, and a few classmates with limited musical experience turned up for a first practice in his family’s kitchen. Fifty years later, the same four played the schoolyard, with students from the school on strings. I don’t know what happens in their rehearsal room. But I know what it takes to keep the same four people in one band for half a century, and it isn’t a clinic. It’s decades of listening to each other.

A band that only plays together on stage finds its problems in front of an audience.

Most organizations run accountability the same way. There’s no weekly room where leaders and managers listen for each other’s cues, so the first time a manager hears the standard clearly is the night it matters, with everyone watching. The course was the clinic. Nobody booked the rehearsal room.

Gallup’s earlier work on why performance management fails shows how common this is: only 50% of employees clearly know what is expected of them at work. One reader summed it up for me in a single line: “A core leadership issue- clarity of expectations horizontally and vertically.” Half the band is guessing the set list. No wonder the accountability conversation feels like an ambush on one side and a necessary evil on the other.

What rehearsal looks like

Gallup’s prescription reads like a rehearsal plan, and it’s just as unglamorous: weekly manager conversations that combine coaching, recognition, priority-setting and discussion of individual strengths. Accountability as a regular, fair discipline, not something saved for corrective moments. The earlier piece sets a specific floor: meaningful feedback every week, substantial developmental coaching every month. Every rehearsal, and a proper lesson once a month.

Start with the set list. Agree on the one or two priorities that matter before you meet again, in words you’d both write down the same way.

Then work the hard passage. Ask what’s stuck, and stay on that one thing instead of touring every project. Coaching is a question about a specific problem, not a speech about general improvement.

Nod when someone nails the fill. Name one thing that went well last week, specifically enough that they could do it again on purpose. Vague recognition sounds like politeness. Specific recognition tells people what the standard is.

Write the parts for the players you have. Once a month, go deeper: ask where their work draws on what they do best and where it grinds against it. Sometimes the fix is adjusting the part, not pushing the player.

And close by checking this week’s set list against last week’s. If the same priority keeps showing up unplayed, that’s the conversation to have now, while it’s still a missed change and not a trainwreck on stage.

What changes when it becomes weekly

Marcel Schwantes flagged this research in Inc. this month, under a headline about how most companies train managers once. The number that should change that habit: the 30% of managers who rate their leader exceptional at accountability are three times as likely to be engaged, 51% versus 17%. These are survey ratings, not performance outcomes, so it’s an association, not proof. But it’s hard to wave away a gap that wide.

In my own work, the shift I see when accountability moves from reaction to rhythm is less dramatic than people expect, and more durable. It stops being a verdict and becomes maintenance. Recognition and correction travel through the same channel, so the correction doesn’t arrive from a stranger. Managers learn what good looks like before they’re judged on it.

One CEO I wrote about in CLUTCH ran a $50 million business with 120 employees and couldn’t take a vacation without his laptop. The first ritual we designed together was small: in his weekly 1:1s, he had to ask three questions before offering a single suggestion.

“What have you already tried?”

“What’s your instinct here?”

“What would you do if I weren’t available to ask?”

He hated it at first. It felt slow. Then one day his CFO said something that stopped him cold: “I’ve started actually preparing for our 1:1s now. I used to bring you problems. Now I bring you options.”

This is why I keep saying leadership is infrastructure, not training. The course isn’t useless. I run professional development sessions too, as every consultant does. But the session was never the system. The real consulting is building structures that keep running after I leave. The system is what happens on an ordinary Tuesday, when nothing is on fire, and you still sit down with the person who manages your people.

One thing to try this week

Most founders assume their expectations are obvious. Here’s how to find out in twenty minutes.

Pick the manager whose work you feel least sure about. Book 20 minutes with them before Friday. Open with one question: “In your own words, what do you think I expect of you this month?” Then listen the way a band listens. Don’t correct them while they talk. Write it down.

Then tell them what you would have said.

Put the two answers side by side. Where they match, say so out loud, because that’s recognition with a standard attached. Where they don’t, that’s the work. Before you leave, agree on one sentence you’d both write down the same way, and read it back to each other.

Then put the next conversation on the calendar for the same time next week. Not because something went wrong. Because that’s when rehearsal is.

U2’s fifty years started with one practice in a kitchen. This is yours.

You’ve just booked the rehearsal room.

The rest of that CEO’s story, including the rituals that stuck, is in the Epilogue of CLUTCH.

item.title: What the auditors couldn't count
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: A watchdog can count awards and positions. It can't count what the people in those positions knew
item.content:encoded:
On September 30, the Government Accountability Office, Congress’s nonpartisan watchdog, published its review of what happened to American foreign assistance after USAID closed.

Most of the report is counting. Between January 2025 and March 2026, about 6,780 of 7,510 USAID awards were terminated. USAID’s workforce went from about 13,600 people worldwide to 241.

Two findings stopped me, and neither of them is a number.

The State Department, which now runs what remains, could not produce data on its own staffing levels during the eleven months the auditors asked for it. It also could not show written guidance, including standards, for how foreign assistance decisions get made.

Read that as an operator. An organization responsible for about $52 billion in active awards could not say who works there or how it decides.

I worked at BHA, USAID’s Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance. I’m not going to argue here about whether the agency should have closed. That’s a policy question, and you have your own view. I want to look at something narrower, because I see it in every kind of organization I work with, from Series B startups to independent schools.

What an audit can’t see

An audit counts what it can count: awards, dollars, positions. It can’t count what the people in those positions knew.

The USAID Employee Support Fund tried. They surveyed their members, and 225 answered. Health officers, agriculture and environment officers, governance specialists, economists, engineers, and the contracting officers who oversaw how the money was spent.

A third of all respondents are unemployed. Of those working again, nearly half have left the field entirely, and about one in four are still in international development or foreign affairs.

The health officers make it concrete. Of the 26 who answered, two still work in international development. Eight have changed fields entirely.

It’s a self-selected sample, not a census. But the direction is hard to miss. The awards moved to State. The knowledge didn’t move with them.

The contracting officer is the control system

Take the contracting officers. On an org chart, a contracting officer looks like administration. In practice, that’s the person who knows why a clause exists, which partner has quietly missed three reports, where the money legally can’t go, and what happened the last time someone tried.

Those are the organization’s controls. They live in someone’s head.

That’s what connects the GAO’s two findings. When the people who made the judgment leave, nothing remains to explain how decisions were made. The GAO warns that, without documented standards, officials risk decisions that are “inconsistent, ad hoc, or inefficient.” Not because the people still there are careless, but because they never wrote the standards down. They didn’t need to be. The people were the standards.

Fast to drain, slow to fill

You probably haven’t lost 98 percent of your staff. But you’ve seen the smaller version. A founder’s first operations hire leaves and takes the vendor history with her. A school loses a division head of twenty years, and the new one discovers the schedule runs on rules nobody wrote down.

What drained wasn’t only oversight. It was application. The officer who knows which roads wash out in the rainy season, so the food has to move by June. The agriculture specialist who remembers which seed variety failed in that valley, and why. The health officer who knows which district clinic reports its numbers on time and which one needs a phone call and a visit. None of that sits in an award file. It’s the difference between money that was spent and money that worked.

Systems thinkers call this a stock. Knowledge accumulates slowly, through years of flow: projects, mistakes, relationships, the third time you see the same problem. A restructuring can drain the stock in an afternoon. Refilling it runs at the original speed, because the only way to learn which roads flood is to be there when they do. That asymmetry is the whole story, and it’s true at any scale.

Headcount is just where the stock happens to be stored. Cut the headcount, and you’ve drained the stock, whether the spreadsheet shows it or not.

Hiring costs more than growing

The Fund put it plainly: “A government cannot buy it back with a hiring announcement.” Neither can a company, and there’s data on why.

Wharton’s Matthew Bidwell studied people hired from outside against people promoted from within into similar jobs. External hires were paid about 18 to 20 percent more, scored lower on performance reviews in their first two years, and were more likely to leave. What they lacked wasn’t talent. It was the firm-specific knowledge and relationships that only time inside builds.

You pay a premium to hire judgment from outside, then wait two years for it to work. Or you grow it, and keep it.

Before you cut, map the load

If you’re about to restructure, ask four questions first.

  1. Which three decisions stall if this person leaves on Friday? If you can’t name them, you don’t know what you’re cutting.

  2. Who else could make each of those calls today, without asking? If the answer is nobody, you’ve found a load-bearing wall.

  3. Who is learning those calls right now? If nobody is, every resignation becomes a restructuring you didn’t plan.

  4. How long would it take you to list who works for you, where they work, and what they own? The State Department couldn’t do it in eleven months. Your answer should be a day.

None of this needs a consultant. It needs someone willing to look at the building before taking out walls.

The GAO made three recommendations to State. Two of them come down to this: know who works for you, and write down how you decide. That advice holds for any organization, whatever its size or mission.

Leadership is infrastructure, not training.

item.title: The manuscript is not the bottleneck
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.content:encoded:
I recently finished a novel that was fine. Competent sentences, a plot that moved, a few scenes I would have cut. Before the author had even finished the manuscript, it had sold film rights. It was a first novel.

I closed it and asked the question every self-published writer asks eventually, usually late at night: how did that happen? Or more precisely: why hasn’t that happened for me?!

Luck? Skill? Both, in proportions nobody publishes.

I’m not asking out of bitterness. Well, not only. If you read this Substack, you know my lane: I help founders build the systems their companies run on. That’s my day job, as I call it. But self-publishing, under my own name and under my pen name, has turned out to be almost like starting a second company. OK, it is starting a second company. Maybe a third.

I’ve put two books into the world through my own imprints, and a third is finished and waiting on its first readers. What I’ve learned is the thing the writing workshops skip. Self-publishing doesn’t make you an author. It makes you a founder. The book is the product. Everything after the last page is distribution, operations, and sales, run by a team of one. Last week I wrote about how I systemized my own work, and this is why, in addition to growing Goode Design & Consulting, I accidentally started a second (or third) company: my nascent publishing empire. I needed a system to run on.

The Martian started as a blog

Andy Weir is the patron saint of people like me. He was a software engineer whose earlier attempt at a novel went nowhere with agents. So he posted The Martian on his own website, chapter by chapter, for free. Readers asked for an ebook. He put it on Kindle for 99 cents, the lowest price Amazon allowed, and it climbed the charts. Then an agent called. Then Crown. Then Fox. Then Matt Damon.

Notice what his readers were doing along the way. They weren’t just reading. They were emailing him corrections to his orbital math. By the time a publisher noticed, a crowd of people already had a stake in that book. That isn’t discovery. That’s a founder with early customers.

People tell Weir’s story as proof that quality rises. Read it again. He built an audience, and the audience did the discovering. The publisher wasn’t betting on Weir. It was buying a result.

The billionaire version

This week The New Yorker reviewed MacKenzie Scott’s new novel, Last Days in Two Nations, which she published in installments on Substack. Plenty of people have wondered aloud why she skipped Amazon. I don’t think it needs much of an explanation.

The review was rough on the craft. But The New Yorker reviewed a self-published, serialized novel, which is more attention than most of us will get in a lifetime. When your name already does the distributing, you can afford to walk away from the biggest bookstore on earth.

The review’s sharper point is that she couldn’t fully escape it anyway. Kindle Direct Publishing built the road most self-published fiction now travels, and even a writer stepping around Amazon is walking through the landscape it made. I’m on that road too. So is every indie author I know. The difference is that most of us don’t get to choose.

Each book taught the next one

Here’s what the founder’s job has looked like, one book at a time. Each one taught me something I used on the next.

  • Balance taught me that a reader is not a review. My first novel, published as m kirk, found good early readers. Then I learned that Amazon doesn’t treat every review the same, and a free early copy can quietly cost you one, no matter how much someone loved it. I had about 20 early readers for Balance, and most of their reviews didn’t show up – they shared them with me – because they never bought the book. I gifted them a copy. Amazon tracks it. I also learned I didn’t own the book’s ISBN, the thirteen-digit number bookstores and libraries use to find it. I’d taken Amazon’s free one, which can’t leave Amazon. Getting the paperback into bookstores and libraries now takes a second distributor and a second ISBN. None of that is writing. All of it decides whether anyone reads.

  • CLUTCH is where I applied those lessons, and found new ways to trip. It’s my leadership book, published under my own name. This time I bought my own block of ISBNs from Bowker, the agency that issues them, so the book’s identity belongs to me, not to Amazon. I launched it at $9.99 to get copies and reviews moving. Then I went live before registering the ISBN, so for its first week on sale, CLUTCH was missing from the catalog booksellers search. I didn’t know I’d missed a step until I went looking. On Amazon, the publisher line reads “m kirk,” my fiction pen name, because of one field Amazon locks the moment you hit publish. Changing it means a support case. That mistake sent me down a road I hadn’t heard of a few months ago: imprints, the publisher name printed on a book’s copyright page and carried in every bookseller’s catalog. I now run two. Tramaridge Press publishes the books under my own name, and The Fern publishes the novels under m kirk, so the two names stop bleeding into each other. Plus copyright. I registered it for CLUTCH. Balance went out before I knew to, so its paperwork is a tangle: the words are mine, but proving it on paper is something the lawyers will need to sort out before Anne Hathaway signs on to play Ellie in the movie. And there’s no Kindle edition of CLUTCH, on purpose: the book asks you to work in it with a pencil. That was a design choice, and it costs me readers every day. I’m OK with that; it was meant to be written in, and an ebook just doesn’t have that kind of vibe.

  • The Wrath of Archie Ellis gets everything the first two taught me. It’s a novel of Passchendaele, 1917, and it’s finished. The ISBN is mine, and this time it gets registered, and the publisher field checked, before I hit publish. I’m also building readers before launch, not after, which is Weir’s lesson. That starts with advance reader copies: free print copies for people willing to read early and post an honest review. On Instagram, I set up an automation: comment YPRES on my pinned post, or message me, and a reply arrives with the request form. Everything I post there also goes to a Facebook author page, and I joined a bunch of historical fiction and WW1 history groups. I have even (gasp) started a TikTok. I hold my nose every time I open it. The US company that now runs it still lists ByteDance as its largest single shareholder, and I’m not naive about where my data goes. But if it sells books, I’ll post.

Writing the books was the part I’d do for free. This is the rest of the job.

I think my novels are good. Not Great American Novel good, but better than some books I’ve read that came with film deals. I mean, they’re at least worth a Booker Short List, though. That matters less than I’d like. A good book nobody finds and a bad book nobody finds sell the same number of copies.

Talent is not a distribution strategy

I see the same pattern with the founders I coach. The best idea in the meeting doesn’t win. The idea with a path does: a sponsor, a forum, a route through the people who decide. Founders who say “the product speaks for itself” are usually the ones whose product nobody has heard of.

Quality is a precondition, not a plan. Weir had readers before he had a publisher. Scott had a name before she had a Substack. Whoever sold that debut novel had a pitch the rest of us never see. In every case, distribution came first, and the craft came along for the ride.

Luck is real. But luck needs somewhere to land. I’m building mine one comment trigger at a time, and this post is part of it.

Read it before anyone else does.

item.title: No job is finished until it leaves a note
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Systems don't break in the middle of the work. They break where it changes hands.
item.content:encoded:
Most work doesn’t get lost while someone is doing it. It gets lost in the gap between one person putting it down and the next person picking it up.

Hospitals learned this the expensive way. A patient’s care changes hands at every shift change, and for a long time that handoff was an informal verbal rundown. When nine pediatric residency programs replaced it with a structured routine called I-PASS, medical errors fell by 23 percent and preventable adverse events by 30 percent. Same doctors. Same patients. The only thing that changed was the handover.

That study stuck with me, because most of the founders I coach have the same problem. Most of them would also tell you they don’t do handovers at all.

You hand off to yourself all day

If you run a practice of one or a few, handovers can sound like a big-company problem. You don’t have shifts. There’s no one to hand to.

But you hand work over constantly. Morning You hands a proposal to Afternoon You. Monday You leaves a half-finished follow-up for Thursday You. The You Who Just Got Off a Client Call hands the next steps to the You Who Will Remember Them, eventually, probably.

Every one of those is a handover. Most of them happen in your head, with no note. That’s the hospital’s informal rundown, minus the hospital.

In my house this is a standing joke. I load the dishwasher, get distracted – squirrel – and forget to start it. I can’t tell you how many mornings I’ve come downstairs wanting coffee and found the French press still sitting in the dishwasher, dirty.

My wife never seems to have this problem. Or maybe she does, and I’ve forgotten, because she can remind me of things from years ago.

That’s a dropped handover. Evening Me did most of the job and handed the last step to nobody. Morning Me paid for it before coffee.

Here’s what the other kind looks like.

Those are book award deadlines for my next novel, WRATH, most of them months away. Fiction isn’t my main business, which is exactly why I would forget every one of them. So each task carries what future me will need: the hard deadline, a start date a week or so earlier, a reminder, and the small decision already made. Books must arrive by 12 February, not merely be posted by it. One copy from the November print order, trade cover only. October Me made those calls, so March Me doesn’t have to dig for them or get them wrong.

That’s a handover across six months, from me to me, and nobody had to remember anything.

You’ll also notice every task has a number. That’s the first of the three choices from my last essay: every task gets a permanent name. The word before the dash says which part of my work it belongs to. The number never changes and never gets reused, even if I rename the task. So a note can say “Done: WRATH-42,” and I can still find it a year from now. One task can point to another by its number. And when a list of questions is waiting on me, I can answer “WRATH-42 is fine, push WRATH-39” instead of explaining which awards thing I mean.

The note at the end of every job

When I built my own system, the rule I’m proudest of is the boring one. No job is finished until it leaves a note.

The note has three parts:

  1. What was done and decided. Two or three sentences, written as a story, not a status. Decisions matter more than activity, because you forget decisions first.

  2. What’s new. Any follow-up the job created goes onto the one shared list, with a name, before the job closes. Not buried in the note. On the list.

  3. What needs me, and what doesn’t. Anything waiting on a decision goes in a short numbered list, so I can answer by number. Everything else is already decided, and the note says so.

The next morning, the notes get read before anything else. That’s the last step in I-PASS, and it may matter most: the person taking over says back what they heard before the handover counts. A note nobody reads is just a diary. Nothing lives only in my head overnight.

The step leaders skip

DELEGATE, the framework in CLUTCH, has eight steps. The one leaders skip most is Transfer: the moment ownership actually changes hands.

Most delegation fails right there. The leader explains the work, sets the expectation, then hands it over in passing. The context stays in their head. Two weeks later, the work comes back wrong, and everyone concludes the person wasn’t ready.

Usually the person was fine. The handover wasn’t. You don’t have a delegation problem. You have a handover problem.

A good handover carries the same three things the note does: what’s already been decided, what’s still open, and what the new owner can decide without asking. That last one is the License. Leave it out, and the work boomerangs back to your desk, because the new owner can’t move without checking.

The same is true when the new owner is future you. If Thursday you doesn’t know what Monday you already decided, Thursday you will either redo the thinking or stall. Both feel like being busy. Neither is progress.

What changed

Here’s a small one. LinkedIn supposedly rewards you for posting the link to your essay a day later, in the comments, rather than with the post itself. I have never once remembered to do that. It’s too small a detail, and by the next day I’m onto something else. So I gave up and pasted the link in the comments as I posted, every time.

It isn’t even creative work. The comment is the same every time: “Click here for the full essay,” and the link. LinkedIn will let you schedule a post, but not a comment on it. So for now the comment gets its own task, with a name and a date, and when I miss it, the miss doesn’t vanish. It’s still on the list the next morning. I’m still working out how to automate the rest.

The surprise for me was that the note isn’t really for the system. It’s for the next person, and most days the next person is me.

Try it this week

You don’t need software for this. Take the next five things you finish this week, and before you call each one done, write three lines:

  1. What did I do, and what did I decide?

  2. What new tasks did this create, and where did I put them?

  3. What still needs a decision, and what can go ahead without one?

  4. If any of those take longer than a minute to answer, you’ve found where your work goes missing.

item.title: Would a system like this help your practice?
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: The path from stranger to conversation, and the three choices that make it work
item.category: Growing faster than it's getting clearer
item.content:encoded:
I mean that as a real question. If you run a practice of one or a few, as a consultant, coach, or founder, and you’ve noticed that everything in the business waits on you, I’d like to know whether what I’m about to describe would be useful to you. I’m not selling anything. I’m trying to find out whether this is worth building for anyone other than me.

Here’s why I’m asking.

Winging it

Most of my working week goes into helping founders get the work out of their heads. Write down the decision. Name the owner. Build the thing that runs when you’re not in the room.

This spring, I admitted I’d always been winging it.

It wasn’t one moment. It was a slow realization. I sell systems thinking, and I hadn’t applied it to my own business. When I had a few clients, I could keep it all in my head. Then the business grew, and the exact thing I help founders through happened to me. I outgrew my own head.

So I built a system, essentially an operating system for the business. I call it GOs, short for Goode Operating System, and because I can’t resist a clever name, it “goes.” It isn’t one new app. It’s a small set of decisions about how the work moves, held together by tools I already used. I see it as a complete ecosystem.

The shape of it

Picture a map. On the left, the audience comes in: people who read something I wrote, see a post, hear me speak. On the right, delivery and money go out: coaching, client work, invoices. In the middle sits a hub, one shared list that every part of the system reads from and writes to.

That’s the whole layout. Everything else is detail about how a person gets from left to right.

Here’s what the two routes below run on:

  • Where people find me. LinkedIn, this newsletter, and my website.

  • Turning interest into contacts. Jotform, Calendly, and Kit.

  • Moving data between them. Zapier.

  • Tasks and records. Airtable as the CRM and Todoist as the one shared list, with Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Calendar alongside.

  • Having the conversation. Google Meet.

Another thirty or so handle delivery, publishing, the websites, and getting paid. That’s about forty tools in all. The tool count is the least interesting thing about the system. It’s also the reason the system needed rules: forty tools with nothing deciding how they connect is just a bigger head.

Two routes, from stranger to conversation

The map has a lot of routes. Two of them matter for this question because together they show how someone goes from never having heard of me to talking with me.

Route one: quiz to CRM. It starts with a LinkedIn post. It includes a link to my leadership quiz, built in Jotform. When someone finishes the quiz, Zapier carries their result into DALE, the CRM I built myself in Airtable. An email sequence in Kit starts. And the lead is scored, so I can see at a glance who is curious and who might want to talk.

My part is the writing. The plumbing does the rest.

Route two: discovery call. Someone books a call through Calendly. A short prep form goes out, so we both arrive knowing why we’re there. The call lands on my Google Calendar with a Meet link. We talk. Afterward, I update the CRM so the conversation doesn’t live only in my memory.

Put the two routes end to end and you have the path from stranger to conversation. Neither route is clever. What makes them work is three choices underneath.

A system is three choices, not a stack of tools

When people hear “system,” they picture software. The software was the easy part. The hard part was deciding three things.

  1. Every task gets a permanent name. Not “that thing for the newsletter.” A name that never changes, so I can point at a job from anywhere and know exactly which one I mean.

  2. Every job has one home. Each kind of work gets done in one place. If two places could own a job, nothing owns it.

  3. The parts only talk to each other through one shared list. No side channels. If a job needs to hand something on, it goes on the list, and the next part picks it up from there.

Notice there isn’t a tool in that list. You could run all three on paper.

This is delegation, pointed at yourself

In CLUTCH I wrote about DELEGATE, my framework for handing work over so it stays handed over. The heart of it is the difference between the Title and the License. You keep the Title: you’re still accountable. You hand over the License: the right to run the work day-to-day, inside guardrails you’ve made clear.

Most solo practitioners never delegate, because there’s no one to delegate to. But you can delegate to a system. The routes above hold the License for the routine work: the follow-up email, the calendar invite, the update to the record. I keep the Title. I decide who I talk to and what I say.

The system is the team member who never forgets.

On AI, since people ask: AI handles the organizing and automating. I do the writing.

What I outgrew

What broke first was me. As a solopreneur, I felt like I was drinking from a firehose. Everything arrived at once, and it all came to me because I was the only place it could go.

The tools followed the same pattern. My CRM started life in Google Sheets, held together with a little JavaScript I wrote myself. That worked until the sheet got more complex than a sheet should be, so I moved it to Airtable. My bookkeeping went the same way. Sheets was my QuickBooks for a while, until I outgrew that too and built a small accounting app in Airtable.

What surprised me was that the bigger fix wasn’t more effort or better apps. It was those three choices. Once every task had a name and a home, the firehose became a list.

So, back to you

Most coaches, consultants, and founders I know run their business the way I ran mine: well, from memory, and a little too late at night. The client work is good. The back office is a person.

So: would a system like this help your practice? Not my exact setup, which is shaped around my odd mix of work. Yours is built on the same three choices you own and run.

If you haven’t built one yet, and you’ve got two minutes, tell me. Six questions. I read every answer, and I’ll only follow up if you say I can.

item.title: Right People, Wrong Seats
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.category: Growing faster than it's getting clearer
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday I argued that coaching for teachers, ranked eighth of thirty school fixes in a New York Times survey of experts, is the reason the top ideas work. Tutoring and the science of reading only change outcomes when someone helps teachers do them well, week after week, in real classrooms.

Whenever I make that case to a school leader, two questions come back. Who would do it? And how would we pay for it?

Here’s my answer to both. Most schools don’t need to hire their coaches. They need to find them.

Right people, wrong seats

In Good to Great, Jim Collins argued that the best organizations start with who, not what: get the right people on the bus, then get them into the right seats. Schools are usually good at the first part. Walk into almost any faculty room and the right people are already there. What schools rarely do is move them.

Every school has teachers who could do this work. Some are close to retirement. Some want to step back from a full load without stepping away. Right now they either leave or carry on quietly in one classroom.

A friend of mine stepped back from full-time teaching and spent several years as a reading specialist. Think of the expertise she carried into one small room at a time. That work mattered. But imagine her working with a small group of teachers instead. That’s a multiplier. Another friend was our building’s expert in critical friends protocols. She ran after-school sessions for colleagues on her own time. She was already doing the job. She just didn’t have the seat.

The seat

The design is simple. Keep one section, so you stay a teacher and stay credible with colleagues. Spend the rest of the week observing, mentoring and coaching.

Then pair the role with your newest teachers. Hand the sections the veteran gave up to an early-career teacher, and let the veteran coach them every week in the classes they just inherited. The new teacher learns the course from the person who knows it best. The veteran who might have retired stays in the building. Every class those two teach gets better.

What they need to learn

This is where schools usually stumble. They find a great teacher, give her a coaching title, and assume the rest takes care of itself. It doesn’t. Coaching is a different craft from teaching, and as yesterday’s research showed, untrained coaches barely move the needle.

The good news is that the gap is specific, and it can be taught. Three distinctions matter most:

  • Observing is seeing what is actually happening in the room, not what the lesson plan says should happen.

  • Mentoring is passing on what you know: here’s how I’d handle that.

  • Coaching, as my own profession defines it, is partnering with someone so they find the answer themselves.

Much of what schools call coaching is really mentoring. Both are valuable. But a teacher who only ever gets advice learns to wait for it. A teacher who gets coached learns to see her own classroom.

This is where professional development finally earns its keep. Not another workshop for the whole faculty on the new program, the kind that fades within weeks. Focused, ongoing training for a small number of the right people, so they become the follow-up for everyone else. Most will take to it quickly. People go into teaching because they love learning, and after twenty years of teaching the same course, a new craft may be exactly the challenge they’ve been missing.

The objection

Every head or school CFO will raise the same objection: we can’t afford another adult in the building who isn’t teaching. It’s a fair point. Most schools already carry more overhead than they’d like. But this isn’t a new position. It’s a teacher you already employ, in a different seat. The real cost is the sections someone else picks up, and when that someone is an early-career teacher paired with the coach who used to teach them, the cost is lower than it looks.

Now set that against a bill you’re already paying. Richard Ingersoll’s research found 44 percent of new teachers leave within five years, and in 2022-23 alone, 30 percent of teachers with two years’ experience or less left their schools. The Learning Policy Institute puts the cost of replacing a public school teacher at up to $25,000 each. In the professional and technical sectors where I do much of my work, I see $60,000 to $80,000, plus nearly two years before a new hire is fully up to speed. Schools rarely see that bill, because it never arrives as one invoice. It hides in the job posting, the interview days, the onboarding, the mentor stipend, and a rookie year spent finding their feet. Then, too often, the teacher leaves, and the school pays it all again.

Keep two early-career teachers from walking out the door, and a hybrid coach pays for her own reduced load. Keep three, and she’s saving the school money.

So the question isn’t whether you can afford a coach. You’re already paying for its absence. And the people are already in your building. The only choice is whether that money keeps leaking out through turnover, or goes into putting the right people in the right seats.

Finding those people, designing the role, and training them in the craft is work I do with independent schools. If you’re weighing it for next year, I’d be glad to talk it through.

item.title: The Eighth Idea
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Experts ranked teacher coaching eighth of thirty ways to fix schools. That’s why the top two work.
item.content:encoded:
Thirty-seven education researchers ranked thirty ways to fix American schools. Then they added a warning: choosing the right idea isn’t enough. None of them work unless schools carry them out well. Duh.

That caveat, tucked into the New York Times ranking last week, is its most important finding. Nobody needs another chart to know American students are slipping, and nobody needs another pilgrimage to Finland to come home with more recess. The Times asked a more useful question: of the things American schools could actually do, what works? Small-group tutoring and the science of reading came out on top, with high-quality preschool, research-backed curriculum, and school accountability also rated highly.

Coaching for teachers came in eighth. I think it belongs on a different list altogether. Coaching isn’t a rival to tutoring or the science of reading, competing for the same budget line. It’s how either of them actually works in a classroom, which is the part the experts said matters most.

We already know this everywhere else. When you want to get into shape, you don’t just buy a gym membership. You hire a trainer. When an executive wants to lead better, they hire a coach. I’m one of those coaches now. Before that, I spent twenty years in schools as a teacher and administrator, which is why I keep coming back to education here. From both sides, the pattern never changes: knowing what works was never the hard part. Doing it well, week after week, with someone watching and adjusting alongside you, is.

Schools have been learning this slowly for a long time. Every wave of reform since A Nation at Risk in 1983, from No Child Left Behind to the post-COVID relief money meant to reinvent school, changed the what: new standards, new tests, new curricula. Almost none changed the how. My friend Jennifer Smith, who has led change in schools for years, draws the line cleanly in her essayYour Initiative Isn’t the Change: an initiative is not change. The initiative is the goal. Change is the slow, collaborative work of getting there, and it’s the part schools keep skipping.

A program is not a practice

The science of reading is a body of evidence about how children learn to decode. Schools learned the hard way what happens when the evidence and the classroom drift apart. For two decades, Lucy Calkins’s Units of Study trained thousands of teachers to have young readers guess at words from pictures and context, a habit the research says belongs to struggling readers. After APM’s Sold a Story brought that to national attention, Calkins revised her materials, Teachers College dissolved her project, and districts including New York City moved away from her approach.

Here’s the part that rarely gets said. Swapping the binder doesn’t swap the habits. A teacher who spent fifteen years prompting “look at the picture” doesn’t unlearn it over a summer. The science of reading becomes a practice only when a second-grade teacher, with twenty-four kids and a fire drill at 10:40, runs a phonics block with fidelity, notices who is stalling, and adjusts. Tutoring is the same. It’s a structure. What happens inside the forty minutes is craft.

Schools usually close that gap with training. A summer workshop, a webinar series, a day of in-service. Then everyone goes back to their classroom alone, and within weeks the new method has eroded into the old habit.

That’s not a teacher problem. It’s a design problem.

Why eighth undersells it

Coaching is the mechanism that turns a program into a practice. In 2018, Matthew Kraft, David Blazar and Dylan Hogan pooled 60 rigorous studies of teacher coaching, and the results are easiest to see if you picture a line of 100 teachers, ranked from weakest to strongest. An average teacher stands at number 50. After coaching, that same teacher moves up to about number 69. That’s roughly the jump from a first-year teacher to one with five to ten years in the classroom, gained without waiting five to ten years.

Now picture 100 students lined up the same way. A typical student in a coached teacher’s class moves from number 50 to about number 57. That may sound modest, but by the researchers’ own yardstick, it sits near the top of what any single change in a school usually delivers. Much of that evidence comes from literacy coaching in the early grades, exactly where the science of reading lives.

Next to tutoring, that student gain looks smaller, and that may be why coaching landed eighth. But the experts scored it as a standalone program. Scored as the thing that makes the top two work, it looks very different. Tutoring reaches the few students at the table. A coached teacher reaches every student she will ever teach.

Even Google had to learn this. A company run by engineers set out to prove its managers didn’t matter, assuming technical skill was what counted. Its own data said otherwise. At the top of its list of what the best managers do: being a good coach. And being a brilliant engineer didn’t make someone good at it. The same is true in schools. Coaching is a different craft from teaching. A teacher who can hold a room of twenty-four seven-year-olds may have no idea how to sit beside a colleague, watch a lesson, and help them see what to change. That skill has to be chosen for, taught, and practiced like any other.

Last week I asked Leadership Lab readers what leadership problem is taking up the most space on their desk. One answer named this essay’s argument better than I could: “Reclaiming the professionalism of the profession of teaching.” Professionals don’t get a workshop. They get watched closely by someone who knows the work, and they get better because of it.

Why it fades at scale

Here’s the catch. The same research found that coaching works best small. In pilot programs with a handful of carefully chosen coaches, the gains were large. When districts rolled coaching out to hundreds of teachers, the gains shrank to a fraction. Other studies find the same story one coach at a time: some coaches change how teachers teach, and some barely move the needle.

That’s not a sign coaching doesn’t work. It’s the fingerprint of an infrastructure failure. The idea holds up. The system built around it doesn’t. Districts hire coaches, then pull them onto testing schedules and lunch duty. One coach ends up responsible for sixty teachers. They were picked for being great teachers, not great coaches, and nobody taught them the difference. With no single focus and no follow-up visit on the calendar, coaching turns into a pleasant chat that changes nothing.

Before the next idea

Kraft, who was one of the experts the Times surveyed, put it plainly: the real lesson isn’t which ideas scored highest. It’s how schools decide.

Schools are very good at deciding. Every summer, somewhere, a leadership team picks a new reading program, a new math curriculum, a new tutoring model. The August in-service is built around it. By spring, the idea that was going to change everything sits on a shelf next to the last one.

The ideas weren’t wrong. Most of them were on the list for good reason. What was missing was the person whose job it was to carry the idea into the classroom, stay beside the teachers using it, and make sure it was still working in October, not just announced in August. That’s not a curriculum decision. It’s a leadership decision, and it’s the one most schools never make.

That’s why the eighth idea matters more than its ranking. The first seven tell you what to do. The eighth explains how to do any of them.

So before your school adopts the next idea on the list, ask two questions. Who will carry it into the classroom? And have you given them the time and the skill to do it well? I’ve turned those into a three-minute check for heads of school and division heads. There’s a second version for parents, too: five questions to ask anyone running for the school board before you vote.

Take the delivery check →

item.title: Your pipeline is a memory problem
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: More systems thinking for small business owners... from a system-thinking small business owner
item.category: Growing faster than it's getting clearer
Winning feels like a near miss
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday I shared a drawing of the system that runs my practice. It got a lot of buzz, several people replied to the short form at the bottom of the post (it’s there again). But the first answer to come in on the form was about the part I’d spent the least time on: DALE, the small gear that brings the work in.

It came from a solo consultant who runs, I gathered, and, as they reported, their business mostly from their head and a notes app. They said everything waits on them. On a bad week, good conversations and real interest never turn into paid work, because every next step depends on them finding the time to take it.

I could have given that answer six months ago.

Most good conversations don’t die from lack of interest. They die in the gap between the call ending and you remembering.

The leak isn’t where you think

Most people running a practice of one assume their revenue problem is about demand. Not enough people know about them. So they post more, speak more, and take more coffees.

Usually demand is fine. The conversations are good. People lean in and say “we should talk about this properly,” and they mean it. Then the call ends, a client emergency lands, and the follow-up waits for a quiet afternoon that never comes. Three weeks later it feels awkward to write. Six weeks later it’s gone.

A handover with nobody on the other end

Relay races are rarely lost on the straights. They’re lost in the exchange zone, the few meters where one runner hands the baton to the next. Good teams drill that handover more than anything else, because that’s where most races go wrong. In swimming, it’s always the false start, not a stroke violation, that DQs a relay. BTW, did you see that Michigan 4x400 relay runner the other day? Wow. Check this out.

A solo practice runs a relay too. The you on Tuesday’s call hands the baton to the you with a free hour on Thursday. Those are two different runners. One knows exactly what was said and why it mattered. The other has forty unread emails and a client deadline. Because both of them are you, nobody drills the exchange. Nobody even marks the zone. You just assume you’ll remember.

That isn’t a sales problem. It’s a handover problem, and the dropped baton is the follow-up.

What the small gear does

DALE stands for Direct Action & Lead Expansion, which is a grander name than it deserves. Actually, I named it after a business coach named Dale, who helped me get my practice off the ground when I suddenly found myself RIF’ed from USAID. It’s the marked zone.

When someone shows interest, I track what they said somewhere other than my head. In practice, that’s Airtable, a database with one table for people and another for the ideas they send me. If they reach out in writing, by email, a comment, or a DM, I keep their exact words and link back to the original so I can reread the whole thing. If it was a conversation in person, it’s my best recollection, written down while it’s still fresh. The rule is simple: if it isn’t in the table, it didn’t happen.

Each entry has a handful of fields. There’s what they’re wrestling with, and what it connects to, whether that’s another reader who said something similar or an essay already on the list. There’s a field for what a useful next step would be for them, which isn’t the same as what would be useful for me. And there’s a credit preference: name them, first name only, anonymous, or ask first.

Every person also sits in exactly one stage, from someone I haven’t contacted yet to someone I’m working with. Nobody is in two stages, and nobody is in none. When I want to know where a conversation stands, I look at the stage, not at my memory.

Then the next step gets drafted. I spend a lot of my time writing. Sometimes it’s a thank-you that names the specific thing they said. Sometimes it’s a note with something useful attached, like an essay that speaks to their problem. Sometimes it’s just a question back.

Every lead also carries a score. I’m purposely not sharing this for now; it’s my secret sauce. No one likes to be objectified as a number on a Likert scale - but anyone who runs a marketing funnel essentially knows: hot, warm, and cold. Once a month, I take a day to look at those scores and check them against what actually happened. Where they were wrong, I change the structure. A score nobody audits is flattery.

What it looked like this week

Over the past week I asked readers a few questions about the leadership problems in front of them.

Before DALE, those would have lived in my inbox, starred, until they weren’t. This time, each idea went into the table in the writer’s own words, next to where it came from and what it might become. Two readers had described the same problem from different chairs, and the table put them side by side. Another pushed back on the premise of an essay I’d planned, which will make it a better essay. I also want to be able to go back and ask them, “Could I use their words in this essay” or, when I finally do write about it, I can cc them and say: Hey, was thinking of you.

Not a capacity problem

The part of that form answer that stays with me is capacity. It’s a real limit, but it points the wrong way. Capacity problems usually get framed as needing more of you: more energy, better habits, another Sunday evening spent catching up.

You don’t have a capacity problem. You have a storage problem. Shocking, it’s a systems issue.

The whole argument of CLUTCH is that leaders should build systems that run without them. That holds for a practice of one too. You don’t need more capacity to follow up. You need follow-up that doesn’t draw on your capacity until the moment you decide.

Try it on paper this week. For years I used just my moleskin, and that was fine until my business grew – more clients, more leads, more balls in the air. I needed… a system. But there is no reason why paper and pencil still don’t work. It’s cheap and fast. Take the last five good conversations you had and write down where the next step for each one lives right now. If the answer is “in my head,” you’ve found the leak. The fix doesn’t need to be clever. It just needs to live somewhere else.

Still asking

Yesterday’s form is still open. If you run a solo or small practice and the small gear sounds like the one you’re missing, raise your hand. It is definitely not one of those cold solicitations that I know we call get: What if we could bring you 12x qualified prospects, we bring you clients, blah, blah. Nope, not that. But it’s a way to track and organize the ones you’re already bringing in.

It’s six questions and takes two minutes. I read every answer, and I’ll only follow up if you say I can. After everything above, you can hold me to that.

item.title: I build systems for leaders. So I drew one up for myself.
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Two loops, thirty projects and one person turning the crank
item.content:encoded:
For about twenty years I’ve told leaders some version of the same thing. If the work only runs when you’re in the room, you haven’t built a system. You’ve built a dependency with your name on it. I wrote a whole book about it. CLUTCH argues that leaders should build systems that run without them.

Since I was RIF’ed from USAID and unexpectedly started a business, I have been building it from scratch as a solopreneur. This August, I took a hard look at my own back office.

Goode Design & Consulting, which helps technical founders scale their businesses. A schools practice, because schools are still my people. Leadership coaching. Several books under two names, each with its own marketing. Two websites, one for the author and one for the business. Several social media accounts. LinkedIn. This Substack. I ran it all on memory and a paper to-do list.

That is the exact setup I spend my working week talking clients out of.

So I drew one up for myself.

It has a name, because everything I build eventually does – it’s the teacher in me.

GOs, short for Goode OS, said “goes.” Two loops sit side by side. The gold one runs the work. The dark one, DALE, brings in the work. Under both run two rails: Todoist, which carries the tasks, and Drive, which carries the story. Where the loops touch, one small circle says Me. That circle is the most honest part of the drawing.

What follows is what I learned building it, and I think most of it travels to anyone running a practice of one or a few.

The parts list

GOs runs on tools most people in my line of work already pay for. Todoist for tasks, Google Drive for documents, and a set of AI workspaces, each holding one kind of work. I use AI to organize and automate the back office, never for my writing or anything creative. The essays, the books, and the coaching are mine.

One of those workspaces is the hub. It reads everything, writes me a morning brief, and runs a sweep every Monday. The rest are spokes: the books, the client practice, the schools work, DALE for revenue, and a few personal things that run the same way.

The spokes stay in their own lanes. That sounds like a flaw. It turned out to be the design.

Two loops

The gold loop is the operating loop. Each morning the hub reads Todoist and Drive and tells me what the day holds. I pick a task. The task says which lane it belongs to, so I work it there. When the job is done, it gets handed over: the task is closed, any follow-ups go into Todoist, and a short note goes into Drive saying what was done and decided. Tomorrow the hub reads the note. Nobody copies and pastes anything, least of all me.

The dark loop is the revenue loop. Someone reads something I wrote, takes a short leadership quiz, and lands in a CRM I built by hand: first in Sheets, with some JavaScript to automate the dull parts, and now in Airtable. DALE has two halves. The builder decides the structure: what I offer, who it’s for, how the CRM is laid out. The runner works inside that structure: reviewing the pipeline and scoring against a running document of my ideal client personas. Once a month, the runner writes field notes for the builder. What people pushed back on. Where the gaps were. Which scores matched what actually happened. The builder changes things. The runner doesn’t.

The same loop runs in a second, quieter mode for finding early readers for the fiction. No scoring there. Nobody reading a novel should be scored. Right now it’s building the advance reader list for Wrath.

Where the two loops touch, there’s me. I decide. That’s the whole job description now, and it’s a smaller job than the one I had.

Four rules that travel

You don’t need my tools for any of these. Most of them work on paper. I still love my Moleskine to-do list – something about filling in those boxes really satisfies me!

  • One owner per task. Every task in GOs carries a permanent code, like CLUTCH-3, and a label naming the lane it belongs to. If two things could own a task, nothing does. The code also lets me refer to any job by name, which matters more than I expected.

  • The tools carry state. People carry decisions. Todoist knows whether a thing is done. Drive knows the story of how it got done. I’m no longer the place where facts live. Anything that needs me comes back as a numbered list, and I answer by number. “Yes to 1, no to 2, 3 can wait” is a morning’s worth of management.

  • Separate whoever builds the system from whoever runs it. When the same hands build and run, the structure drifts every time a Tuesday gets hard. Split the roles, even if you play both on different days.

  • Learn monthly, against real results. The field notes are the only reason DALE gets better, not just busier. A score nobody checks against what happened is a guess with decimals.

What still creaks

It’s a few weeks old, and it isn’t finished.

Each part of the work runs on its own and learns about the others only from what gets written down. That keeps things clean, and it means the handover notes carry the whole load. When one is lazy, the next morning is too. Some of it still needs me at the keyboard, doing by hand what should run by itself. And I still turn the crank. The system doesn’t decide what matters this week. It clears away everything except that decision, which is the point, but the crank does not turn itself.

A question for you

Most coaches and consultants I know run their practice the way I ran mine: well, from memory, and slightly too late at night. The work is good. The back office is a person.

So I’m thinking about turning this into something other coaches can use. Not my exact setup, which is built around my odd mix of work. Yours, built on the same rules and set up around your practice, that you own and run. If it works for enough people, I’ll probably charge for it. But mostly I want other coaches to get their evenings back.

I don’t have anything to sell you yet. I have a drawing, a system that works for one person, and a question: would you want one?

If you run a solo or small practice and you’d want a system like this for your own work, raise your hand. Six questions, two minutes. Your answers will shape what I build, and whether I build it at all. I read every answer, and I’ll only follow up if you say I can.

item.title: The Title and the License
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Your best person has the job. Find out whether they have the authority.
item.content:encoded:
There is a moment I have watched happen in a dozen companies, and it always looks like a promotion.

A founder hands someone the thing. Vendor relationships, the hiring plan, the product line, the P&L for a region. It is said warmly and it is meant warmly. You own this now.

Six weeks later that person is in the founder’s office asking whether they can spend eleven thousand dollars.

They own it. They just cannot do anything with it.

Two different things wearing one word

When we say delegation, we usually mean one act. It is two, and most organizations only ever perform the first.

A Title is the name on the work. It is who gets asked about it in the standup, whose name is on the slide, who is understood to be responsible when it goes wrong.

A License is the authority to make decisions about it. The budget, the scope, the vendor choice, the calendar, the right to say no to a request from someone senior.

Title is cheap and it feels generous. License is expensive, because giving it away means you will occasionally watch someone make a call you would not have made, and live with it.

So we give the Title and keep the License, and then we are puzzled that the person is not stepping up.

Why this is the accountability problem

Lencioni argues, correctly, that the strongest accountability in a team runs sideways rather than downward. Peers holding peers to the standard beats a manager doing it, every time.

But peers cannot hold each other to work nobody actually owns.

Watch what happens in a team where Titles have been handed out and Licenses have not. Someone’s project slips. A peer notices. And the peer does the arithmetic in about half a second: is this person actually able to fix this, or are they waiting on the founder like the rest of us? If the answer is waiting, the peer says nothing, because calling someone out for a delay they have no power to prevent is just cruelty with a process attached.

So accountability becomes theater. The person with the Title can be blamed. They cannot act. Their peers sense this and hold back, and they are right to.

The team is not conflict-avoidant. The team is being accurate.

The eleven thousand dollar test

Here is a diagnostic you can run this week without telling anyone you are running it.

Pick something you believe you have delegated. Then answer these four, on paper, before you ask the person:

  1. What is the largest amount of money they can commit without asking you?

  2. Can they say no to a request from someone more senior than they are, and would that no hold?

  3. Can they change the deadline, or only report on it?

  4. If they hire the wrong person into their team, who do you believe made that mistake?

Then ask them the same four questions and compare.

The gap between your answers and theirs is the size of the problem, and it is almost always larger than the founder expects. I have never once seen a founder guess low.

Question four is the one that does the work. If you hear yourself say that you would have made the call differently, you never handed over the License. You handed over the blame.

What a real handoff contains

A License transfer is boring on purpose. It is four sentences, written down, in the place the work lives:

  • The decision rights. What they can decide alone, what they decide and tell you, what they bring to you first. Name the dollar figure.

  • The boundary. What is explicitly not theirs, so that a no from them is a real no.

  • The reporting line. What you want to know and when, which is not the same as what you want to approve.

  • The reversal rule. Under what conditions you will overrule them, agreed in advance and in daylight.

That last one is the one people skip, and it is the one that makes the rest credible. Everyone knows you can overrule them. Saying when converts an unpredictable risk into a known one, and people will take risks against a known rule that they will not take against a mood.

The part this costs you

I will not pretend this is free.

The first time someone spends the eleven thousand on something you would not have bought, you will feel it. You will have a private thought about whether they are ready. That thought is the actual test, and it is a test of you.

Because the alternative is the thing you already have. A team of capable adults with impressive Titles, all waiting outside your office, and a calendar that proves you are indispensable.

Indispensable is not a compliment. It is a diagnosis.

The DELEGATE framework in CLUTCH is the handoff, step by step: what transfers, what you keep, and how to know it landed.

item.title: I kept the shelf and enforced the policy
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Better talent identification makes the problem worse
item.category: Growing faster than it's getting clearer
item.content:encoded:
I kept a bookshelf in my room at McDonogh. Not a library, not a program. A shelf, in the room where I met my middle school advisees, stocked with whatever I thought might land on somebody. Novels, comics, books about cars.

Our librarians were excellent, and most of what sat on that shelf came from asking them what to get. But a kid had to walk to the library, and the librarians couldn't be everywhere. The shelf didn't need anyone to walk anywhere. It was already in the room.

One of my advisees hated reading and loved baseball, so I handed him Heat. He read it. Then he read the next one.

Nothing about that required him to be anything first. No reading level, no referral, no conversation about what he'd struggled with. He liked baseball, there was a book about baseball, and the shelf was right there.

Meanwhile the school ran DEAR. Drop Everything And Read, Thursdays, everyone at once, building-wide. I don't know a better way to make a kid hate reading than to require it on a schedule. But to support my English colleagues… (but the math teacher and I would often quip, when is “drop everything and do equations!” day?)

And once reading was “mandatory, not reading became misconduct. I was also the Dean. So I was the one standing there asking, "Why don't you have a book today?"

I hated that part.

Here's the part that should bother you.

Your company has a DEAR. Several, probably. Mandatory training, a development framework, a mentoring program with an application form. It probably also has good people whose whole job is helping other people get better, the way our librarians were good.

What it may not have is anyone's shelf. The question was never whether the expertise exists. It's whether someone has to cross the building to reach it.

Run the list. Who gets a mentor? Someone a manager put forward. Who gets the stretch assignment? Someone already on the list. Who gets the development budget? Someone whose last review cleared a bar. Who gets coached? Either a star or a problem, and the conversation that decided which one is a conversation you weren't in.

You'll want to say this is what a finite budget looks like. That gates allocate scarce development toward expected return, and that's arithmetic, not a moral failure.

That defense would hold if gates measured expected return. They measure legibility. A gate sorts for who's readable by the instrument you happen to own, and the distance between readable and valuable is far wider than the people running the gate believe. My advisee wasn't a reluctant reader. He was a baseball reader in a building with no instrument for baseball readers.

Now the harder part. You cannot audit this by looking at who you developed. You can only look at who you did not, and those people are, by construction, the ones you have no data on.

Except that isn't quite true, and it's where most leadership teams stop too early. The missing leave traces. Start with who volunteers for the optional things, then write down five capable people who never appear on any of those lists. Somewhere between year two and year four you'll find people who haven't changed role or scope in eighteen months and aren't underperforming; they're still employed, which is exactly what makes them invisible. Internal transfer records will tell you who applied twice and then stopped. And in an exit interview, the useful answer arrives around the twenty-minute mark, once the rehearsed part is done.

None of that measures the people you missed. All of it measures the shape of the hole.

And the standard remedy makes the hole bigger. When a leadership team senses it's missing people, the reflex is to improve identification: a better talent review, tighter calibration, clearer criteria for who counts as high potential. All of that sharpens the instrument. None of it reaches the person the instrument can't read. You can calibrate a gate for a decade, and it's still a gate.

What helps is one thing in the building with no gate on it.

Not a program. Programs have intake. One ungated thing, reachable without a nomination, a rating, or somebody's yes. Office hours anyone can book, three levels down included, not routed through a manager. A channel where people put a hand up for work before anyone has assessed whether they should. A budget line small enough to need no business case.

It'll feel inefficient. That's the price. The gates were installed to prevent exactly this waste, and they do. They also prevent the other thing.

The gate audit

  1. Name every route to support, growth, or visibility here. For each, write down what is required to get in.

  2. How many require someone else's judgment first? A nomination, a rating, a manager's yes.

  3. What is left with nothing in front of it? If the answer is nothing, that is the finding.

  4. Build one ungated thing this quarter. Then name the person who has to agree never to put a gate on it later.

The fourth is the real work. Ungated things don't stay ungated. They accumulate criteria quietly, because every individual criterion is sensible and whoever adds it is trying to help.

My shelf stayed open because nobody ever wrote it down. That's also why it left when I did.

Most of your people are fine inside the gates. They get nominated, they clear the bar, the system finds them.

Pick one route this week and write down what it costs to enter. You'll know straight away whether anyone here keeps a shelf.

If you want to run all eleven, the gate check is here. Two minutes, nothing to sign up for.

If you know someone who runs the gates in their building, send them this.

item.title: The Pyramid and the Drivetrain
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Lencioni mapped the downward spiral. Here’s how to build the upward one.
item.content:encoded:
I was in a colleague’s office recently and noticed The Five Dysfunctions of a Team on his bookshelf. It had the soft spine of a book that’s been read more than once.

Seeing it brought back a question I worked through while writing CLUTCH. If Lencioni gave us such a clear map of how teams break, why do so many teams that have read the book stay broken?

Patrick Lencioni’s 2002 fable has probably been handed to more new managers than any leadership book of the last twenty-five years. It endures because it names something every team has felt: teams rarely fail because of a lack of talent. They fail from a chain of avoidance, one step at a time.

My answer is that the pyramid tells you what is going wrong. It doesn’t tell you what to build to stop it.

The cascade, briefly

Without trust, teams avoid conflict and settle into artificial harmony. Without honest conflict, nobody truly commits. Without commitment, nobody holds peers accountable. Without accountability, individual status beats team results. The fable’s fix is mostly about behavior: the leader goes first, shows vulnerability, draws out conflict, and holds the standard. Lencioni’s later work, especially The Advantage, moves toward structure, but the fable is the book on the shelves.

That’s where CLUTCH picks up.

Where the two books meet

CLUTCH argues that leadership bottlenecks are design problems, not effort or character problems. When a team keeps stalling in the same place, it’s usually missing something that would make the right behavior easy. Read that way, each level of the pyramid points to a part of the drivetrain that is missing or slipping.

  • Trust erodes when ownership is unclear. It rarely goes in one dramatic betrayal. When nobody knows who owns what, people protect themselves, and self-protection is the opposite of vulnerability. Asking a team to be more open while leaving ownership vague is asking them to take a risk the structure keeps punishing. In CLUTCH, this sits in the engine: trust is an outcome you design for, not a feeling you hope for.

  • Conflict is where behavior still does the most work. Most teams that avoid conflict aren’t cowardly. They’ve learned that disagreement costs more than it’s worth, because the person with the most power reacts badly to it. The fix is to engineer safety for dissent: make it easy for someone to say “I’m not sure that’s right,” then thank them, whether or not you act on it. If no one has pushed back on you in the last month, it isn’t because there’s nothing to push back on. Quiet rooms aren’t aligned rooms. This is why CLUTCH treats emotional intelligence as the clutch, the part that lets a team change gears without grinding them. It’s the one level where design can’t fully replace the leader.

  • Commitment dies after the debate, not during it. I cite Lencioni by name in the 6C chapter because he traces lack of commitment to unresolved conflict and unclear decision rights. The second half of that gets less attention than it should. People leave the room unsure whether they were consulted, whether they had a vote, or whether the call was made before the meeting started.

The 6C Decision Compass closes that gap by naming the mode before the discussion: Command, Consultative, Collaborative, Consensus, Core Expert, or Choice. Someone overruled in a clearly named Consultative decision can still commit, because the process did what it said it would. Someone overruled in what they thought was a Consensus decision checks out quietly. Same decision, different outcome. The only difference was clarity about how it would be made.

  • Accountability needs a License, not just a Title. Lencioni rightly argues that the strongest accountability runs between peers. But peers can’t hold each other to work nobody owns, and most organizations have work that's assigned but not handed over. A Title is the name on the task. A License is the authority to make decisions about it: the budget, the scope, the right to say no. When someone has the Title without the License, accountability becomes theater. They can be blamed, but they can’t act. Their peers sense this and hold back, and they’re right to. The DELEGATE framework transfers both.

  • Results follow what the system rewards. When one heroic person keeps saving the quarter, the team learns that results belong to the hero. When wins count as team wins, the output feeds back into the engine as trust. That’s the flywheel: what the system produces becomes what it runs on.

The reverse cascade

Trust enables candor. Candor sharpens decisions. Decisions build accountability. Accountability generates results. Lencioni showed the downward spiral. Design builds the upward one.

The cascade runs in both directions. Every clean handoff reinforces trust. Every clearly named decision makes the next disagreement safer.

Where they differ

The two books aren’t saying the same thing, and pretending otherwise flattens both.

In the fable, Kathryn turns her team around by modeling vulnerability, holding the line, and refusing to let artificial harmony win. That’s real. But a fix that depends on the leader’s courage in every meeting has a ceiling. It works while that leader is in the room and has the energy. CLUTCH is written for the moment that stops working: the founder at 60 people who can’t be in every conversation, or the head of operations holding the culture together alone.

So the question I’d add to Lencioni’s is this. You’ve modeled the behavior. What have you built so it survives when you’re not there?

If the book is on your shelf too

Take down your copy and pick the level of the pyramid where your team stalls most often. Then, instead of asking who needs to behave differently, ask what is missing from the design.

Is ownership unclear enough that vulnerability feels risky? Are decisions made without anyone naming how they’ll be made? Are people carrying Titles without Licenses?

The dysfunction is the symptom. The design is the fix. That’s the difference between a team that has read the book and a team that no longer needs it.

Put CLUTCH next to Lencioni on the shelf.

CLUTCH: How Leaders Build Systems That Run Without Them is the design manual for those questions. It gives you four frameworks for building a team that runs without you: CREATE, 6C, VOICES, and DELEGATE.

It’s a working book, made for a pencil, so it comes in paperback.
